content: A pentose is a type of monosaccharide that contains five carbon atoms. These molecules can be classified based on the functional group they possess. If the functional group is an aldehyde located at the first carbon atom, the pentose is referred to as an aldopentose. Conversely, if the functional group is a ketone located at the second carbon atom, the pentose is classified as a ketopentose. Aldopentoses have three chiral centers, which are carbon atoms bonded to four different groups, making them asymmetric. Due to this, there are eight possible stereoisomers of aldopentoses. Among these, the four naturally occurring D-aldopentoses are ribose, arabinose, xylose, and lyxose. A mnemonic to help remember these four D-aldopentoses is ribs are extra lean. Ketopentoses, on the other hand, have two chiral centers, resulting in four possible stereoisomers. These include ribulose and xylulose, each of which exists in both Dand L-forms. The D-isomers of ribulose and xylulose are naturally occurring, as is the L-isomer of xylulose. The aldehyde group in aldopentoses and the ketone group in ketopentoses can react with nearby hydroxyl groups within the same molecule. This reaction forms intramolecular hemiacetals in aldopentoses and hemiketals in ketopentoses. The resulting cyclic structures resemble a furan ring and are therefore referred to as furanoses. These ring structures are not static; they can spontaneously open and close. During this process, rotation occurs around the bond between the carbonyl carbon and the adjacent carbon atom, leading to the formation of two distinct configurations, known as the alpha (α) and beta (β) forms. This phenomenon is called mutarotation. Ribose, one of the aldopentoses, is a critical component of ribonucleic acid (RNA). A closely related sugar, deoxyribose, which is derived from ribose by the removal of an oxygen atom, is a fundamental component of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA).
